title: The Market System — The Economic Problem
summary: Scarcity exists because wants are unlimited but resources are finite. This means choices have to be made. Every choice has an opportunity cost. A PPC / PPF shows the maximum possible combinations of two goods an economy can produce. Points on the curve are efficient, points inside show unemployment of resources, and points outside are unattainable. An outward shift shows positive economic growth. An inward shift shows negative economic growth.

title: The Market System — Economic Assumptions
summary: Economists assume that consumers try to maximise benefit and firms try to maximise profit, but in real life they do not always do this. Consumers may copy others, follow habits, or make poor decisions. Firms may care about customers, workers, reputation, sales, or charity rather than only profit.

title: Demand Curve
summary: Quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices.

title: Factors that Shift Demand
summary: Income, substitutes, complements, advertising, and tastes.

title: Supply Curve
summary: Quantity producers are willing and able to sell at different prices.

title: Factors that Shift Supply
summary: Costs, taxes, subsidies, technology, and weather.

title: Market Equilibrium
summary: Market equilibrium is where demand equals supply. The equilibrium price and quantity are determined by market forces. If price is above equilibrium, there is excess supply. If price is below equilibrium, there is excess demand. Market forces remove shortages and surpluses by changing price.

title: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED)
summary: PED measures how much demand responds to a price change. It also determines total revenue.

title: Price Elasticity of Supply (PES)
summary: PES measures how responsive supply is to price changes.

title: Income Elasticity of Demand (YED)
summary: YED shows how demand changes when income changes.

title: Mixed Economy & Market Failure
summary: A mixed economy has both a private sector and a public sector. The private sector is made up of businesses owned by individuals or shareholders. The public sector is owned or funded by the government. Governments intervene when markets do not allocate resources efficiently. This is called market failure.

title: Privatisation
summary: Privatisation means transferring ownership of a business from the public sector to the private sector. Governments may privatise to raise money, improve efficiency, or reduce the size of the public sector. The effects are mixed: some groups may benefit and others may lose out.

title: Externalities
summary: Externalities are costs or benefits that affect third parties who are not directly involved in the activity. External costs are negative spillover effects. External benefits are positive spillover effects. Because of this, markets may overproduce some goods and underproduce others.

title: Factors of Production & Sectors of the Economy
summary: All production needs the four factors of production: land, labour, capital, enterprise. Economies are divided into the primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors. As countries develop, employment and output usually move away from primary and towards tertiary.

title: Productivity & Division of Labour
summary: Productivity measures how efficiently resources are used. Labour productivity is usually output per worker. Division of labour means splitting a production process into smaller tasks so workers specialise. This can raise output, but it can also make work boring.

title: Business Costs, Revenue and Profit
summary: Businesses need to calculate revenue, costs, and profit. Revenue is the money coming in. Costs are the money going out. Profit is what is left after costs are taken away from revenue.

title: Economies and Diseconomies of Scale
summary: When a firm grows, it may become more efficient and reduce average costs. These are economies of scale. But if it grows too much, problems may appear and average costs may rise. These are diseconomies of scale.

title: Competitive Markets
summary: A competitive market has many firms selling similar products. No single firm can control the price, so they must accept the market price.

title: Large and Small Firms
summary: Firms can be large or small, and each has advantages and disadvantages depending on the market and goals.

title: Monopoly
summary: A monopoly is a market where one firm dominates and has significant control over price.

title: Oligopoly
summary: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms that are interdependent.

title: The Labour Market — Demand and Supply
summary: Hiring, labour supply, and the equilibrium wage.

title: The Labour Market — Trade Unions
summary: Collective bargaining, wages, and employment.

title: Government Intervention
summary: Governments intervene in markets to correct market failure, reduce negative effects, and improve outcomes for society.

title: Economic Growth
summary: Economic growth is an increase in the output of goods and services in an economy over time.

title: Inflation
summary: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level over time.

title: Unemployment
summary: Unemployment occurs when people who are willing and able to work cannot find jobs.

title: Balance of Payments (Current Account)
summary: The current account records a country’s trade in goods and services and income flows.

title: Protection of the Environment
summary: Economic activity can damage the environment, creating negative externalities. Governments intervene to reduce these effects.

title: Redistribution of Income
summary: Governments redistribute income to reduce inequality and poverty.

title: Fiscal Policy
summary: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation to influence economic activity.

title: Monetary Policy
summary: Monetary policy controls interest rates to influence inflation and economic growth.

title: Supply-Side Policies
summary: Supply-side policies aim to increase productivity and long-run economic growth.

title: Relationships Between Objectives and Policies
summary: Macroeconomic objectives can support each other, but they can also conflict. Governments often face trade-offs when trying to reduce unemployment, control inflation, achieve economic growth, protect the environment, and improve the current account.

title: Globalisation
summary: Globalisation is the increasing integration of economies through trade, investment, migration, communication, and technology. It affects countries, firms, workers, consumers, governments, and the environment.

title: Multinational Companies and Foreign Direct Investment
summary: Multinational companies operate across countries and often bring foreign direct investment. They can increase jobs, output, and skills, but may also create problems such as profit outflows and pressure on local firms.

title: International Trade
summary: International trade allows countries to specialise, sell abroad, and buy goods and services from other countries. It can improve efficiency and living standards, but also create risks for domestic industries.

title: Protectionism
summary: Protectionism is the use of trade barriers to reduce imports and protect domestic industries. It may help local producers, but often raises prices and reduces efficiency.

title: Trading Blocs
summary: Trading blocs are groups of countries that reduce trade barriers between members. They can increase trade and growth for members, but may disadvantage non-members.

title: The World Trade Organization and World Trade Patterns
summary: The WTO encourages free and fair trade and helps resolve trade disputes. Trade patterns differ between developed and developing countries.

title: Exchange Rates and Their Determination
summary: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. Exchange rates are determined by demand for and supply of currencies.

title: Impact of Changing Exchange Rates
summary: When exchange rates change, the prices of exports and imports change. This affects trade, inflation, growth, and the current account.
